newsitem.title: USA: Dirty laundry to be aired at Senate hearings.
newsitem.headline: Dirty laundry to be aired at Senate hearings.

text.p: A Senate investigation into political fund-raising scandals in last year's campaigns finally opens this week with both Republicans and Democrats bracing for a lengthy airing of dirty laundry.

Once Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson raps the gavel Tuesday to start oversight hearings of his Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, Americans will be treated to a four-week spectacle that may liven up the summer doldrums. Thompson says his goal will be "following the allegations and following the evidence, wherever that might be."

At stake could be the credibility of President Clinton, whose approval ratings have remained favourable despite criticism he has drawn for fund-raising tactics including the use of White House perks such as sleepovers for big donors in the Lincoln Bedroom.

Vice President Al Gore, who aspires to succeed Clinton in the 2000 election, could also take some public relations hits. His role in a questionable Democratic fund-raiser at a Buddhist temple last summer will also be examined.

The White House has cried foul in the run-up to the hearings, accusing Thompson of a biased approach that has not focused as hard on Republican campaign finance abuses. "Sheer partisan politics," griped one White House aide.

Thompson, the smooth-talking former actor who was chief minority counsel during the Senate Watergate hearings in the 1970s, vowed a fair inquiry but made clear Democrats would get the brunt of the attention because most of the allegations so far have been made against them.

"I'm not going to try to generate a lot of time and effort just trying to find something in the name of so-called balance," he told CNN. "Whatever the allegations are, that should be the determining factor and not which party is producing the allegations."
Committee spokesman Paul Clark said Thompson's goal was "to inform the American public about what happened in a year in which we've seen so many serious allegations of fraud and corruption."

"Our job is not to prosecute anybody or put anybody into jail. It's to inform," Clark said, hinting that some new allegations could surface in the hearings beyond what has been reported in the months since Clinton's re-election.

A top priority of the hearings is to determine whether China and other foreign interests sought to influence U.S. foreign policy by helping Clinton and the Democratic Party with illegal political contributions.

Complicating that goal is the expected absence of two key players: John Huang, a former Commerce Department official who moved to the Democratic National Committee to raise money, and Charles Yah Lin Trie, a former Arkansas restaurant owner and longtime friend of Clinton.

The two men raised nearly $4 million from Asian-American sources but the Democratic National Committee has returned $1.6 million in questionable contributions raised by Huang and $645,000 donated or raised by Trie.

Huang has made clear he would invoke the Fifth Amendment against self-incrimination if called to testify, but he still might be forced to appear. Trie, who lives in China now, has said he would refuse to testify. "They'll never find me," he said in an NBC interview from Shanghai recently.
But Thompson said their lack of cooperation would not deter him.

"I think it's important that the committee lay out the facts that it can, give depth and perception, the facts that are already on the record, and paint a picture," Thompson said Sunday on the "ABC This Week" television programme.

"And Sam Ervin used to say that if you could paint a real good picture of a cow, you didn't need to write the word 'cow' under it," he said, invoking the name of the North Carolina Democrat who chaired the 1973 Senate Watergate hearings.

The absence of testimony from Huang and Trie will likely lead Republicans to direct questions about them to Harold Ickes, who was Clinton's deputy chief of staff and de facto campaign chairman last year, and Don Fowler, the DNC's former co-chairman, among others.
Ickes and Fowler have been subpoenaed to testify, as have long-time Clinton confidant Bruce Lindsey and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton's former Chief of Staff Maggie Williams.

White House aides who plan an aggressive counter-assault against allegations made in the hearings say they believe Republicans for the most part will simply be going over ground that has already been covered in countless newspaper articles.
Both sides said they hoped the whole process would lead to a reform of the way political parties raise huge sums to finance campaigns.

That outcome would be welcomed by the independent watchdog group Common Cause, which has long sought to ban large, unregulated contributions called "soft money" that get around federal limits on individual donations.

"One of the things that we hope is made clear is that virtually all of the potential illegalities and improprieties during the last presidential race resulted from the soft money system," Common Cause President Ann McBride said.
